newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to hold firm on expanding NATO - Albright.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to hold firm on expanding NATO - Albright.

text.p: Taking a hard line ahead of the U.S.-Russia summit in Helsinki, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Tuesday that NATO expansion would proceed despite Russian objections and the United States would not "bargain away" Central Europe.

Briefing reporters on the meetings this Thursday and Friday between President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Finland, Albright said that although Russia deserved a voice on European security, it would get no veto.

In comments filled with references to the Cold War, which she stressed was over, the Czech-born secretary said the NATO expansion would proceed with or without Moscow's approval. She asserted that the West was under no pressure to reach a formal accord with Russia on that point at the Helsinki summit.

"NATO enlargement will remain on track," she said. "New allies will enjoy the full benefits and assume the full responsibilities of membership. The first new members will not be the last and we will exclude no European democracy from future consideration."

"I can assure you that (neither) the president nor I are going to bargain away the rights of the Central Europeans, said Albright, whose family fled Czechoslovaka shortly after World War II. "Neither justice nor history will allow that."

Saying the United States and Russia were partners, rather than adversaries, Albright added that "Russia, in fact, does have a seat at the table in discussions on Europe, but not a veto over the decisions."
Expanding NATO, long resisted by Russia, is expected to be one of the thorniest issues at the summit, the first between Clinton and Yeltsin in a year.
The NATO plan is to invite new members to join the 16-member alliance at a summit in Madrid in July, with Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic the leading candidates.

Albright's remarks appeared something of a rebuff to Yeltsin, who said in a television interview on Sunday that Russia could not make any further concessions and was worried about economic and strategic isolation.

"'Concessions' is an inappropriate word," Albright said when asked about Yeltsin's remarks. "This is a discussion about how to have the Russians cooperate in a new European atmosphere and ... to make clear that the countries that were, are, in a gray zone in Central Europe no longer are there."

She rejected the idea that she was simply laying down a negotiating stance before the summit. "We are not taking any rhetorical positions," she said. "We are not bargaining away the rights of the Central Europeans who were, to a great extent, the victims of the Cold War, and what President Clinton has said is what he is trying to do is to eliminate the dividing line through the centre of Europe."
But she also stressed that Washington and Moscow, despite disputes, now operate as partners rather than adversaries.
"It's very important not to look at this summit ... as far as the European security issues are concerned, as a zero-sum game," she said. "It is not us versus them or them versus us."

Marking out the dates that essentially chart the course of the Cold War, Albright added: "We do not face a choice between diminishing NATO or diminishing Russia. It is not 1949 or 1989. Today we are all on the same side."
Albright, who will accompany Clinton to Finland, has held intensive talks over the last few days in Washington with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.
She said the United States was intent on NATO's negotiating a separate charter with Russia to set out their future relations, but there was no deadline for this.

"The point of the charter is to advance an enduring interest NATO and Russia will continue to share ... For this reason, while we would welcome agreement in the next few months, there is no deadline, not in Helsinki or in Madrid. The door will stay open."

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns expanded on that key point later, saying "substantial" work remained to be done on the Russia-NATO charter and the expectation was "that it will not be possible to complete all that work by Friday evening and that Helsinki is a step towards Madrid."

"There is still no assurance that NATO and Russia will agree on a charter," he added. " ... And if by the end of June, or early July there is no charter worked out then NATO will simply go ahead with its plans to expand."
NATO would prefer an accord with Moscow, he said, but added: "It takes two to tango."
